# Volume 1 — CHAPTER XXXV. The Winter at Regent’s

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Her weekend trips to her house were a big assistance in fading away NELL’S longing for home. Every Friday evening, provided the mild weather continued, those who attended Brierley took the new branch line to travel to Delford. A cheerful group of them would all journey to Brierley on foot after Isolde, along with various other Brierley youths, usually arrived to greet them. Nell felt that the finest and sweetest times of the entire week were those Friday night rambles through the cool, bright air across the autumn hills, while the lights of home in Brierley shimmered in the distance.
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0000 }

Almost all the time, Hugh Carrow accompanied Opal Pettigrew on her walks and tote her bag for her. Opal was a most attractive young woman, who at present considered herself just as mature as she actually was; her skirts were worn as long as her mother permitted, and her hair was styled up while she was in town, even though she was required to let it down upon returning home. Her eyes were big and vivid blue, her skin radiant, and her shape full and eye-catching. She indulged in much laughter, maintained a sunny and pleasant disposition, and openly delighted in the enjoyable aspects of living.
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0001 }

“However, I don’t believe she is the kind of girl Hugh would enjoy,” Odette murmured in a whisper to Nell. Nell shared that opinion, yet not even the Avery scholarship would have induced her to express it. Furthermore, she was unable to avoid thinking that possessing a friend like Hugh would be delightful, allowing one to joke, talk idly, and trade thoughts regarding books, studies, and future goals. Hugh possessed goals, as she was aware, and Opal Pettigrew appeared not to be the type of individual with whom a person could gainfully converse about them.
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0002 }

Nell entertained no foolish sentimentality regarding her thoughts on Hugh. To her mind, on the rare occasions she considered them, boys were simply potential good companions. Had a friendship existed between herself and Hugh, the number of his other companions or the identity of his walking partners would not have mattered to her. Friendship was her natural talent; while she possessed numerous female friends, she felt an indistinct awareness that male comradeship could likewise prove beneficial in completing one's ideas of fellowship and providing wider viewpoints for evaluation and comparison. Naturally, Nell would have been unable to express her sentiments on the topic in precisely those explicit terms. Nevertheless, she believed that had Hugh ever accompanied her on the journey home from the train, across the frosty meadows and down the fern-lined lanes, they could have engaged in numerous cheerful and captivating discussions concerning the emerging realm expanding before them, alongside their personal aspirations and desires within it. Hugh was a smart youth who possessed individual perspectives on matters, coupled with a resolve to extract the finest elements from existence while contributing his utmost to it. Opal Pettigrew informed Odette Pullen that she failed to comprehend half of the statements made by Hugh Carrow; he conversed in the exact manner as Nell Harcourt during one of her reflective moods, and as far as she was concerned, she found no enjoyment in troubling herself with literature and similar topics when it was not required. Frank Stockley exhibited much superior energy and spirit, yet he lacked even half of Hugh’s attractive appearance, leaving her truly incapable of determining which one she preferred!
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0003 }

Within the Academy, Nell slowly gathered around herself a small group of companions, who were contemplative, creative, and driven scholars just like she was. She quickly grew close to Mabel Colby, the “rose-red” girl, and Honora Hollis, the “dream girl,” discovering that this last fair, ethereal-appearing young woman was thoroughly packed with mischief, jokes, and humor, whereas the striking, dark-eyed Mabel possessed a heart brimming with yearning dreams and imaginations, which were as light and multicolored as those belonging to Nell herself.
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0004 }

When the Christmas holidays ended, the students at Brierley stopped returning home on Fridays and devoted themselves to rigorous study. By then, every scholar from Regent’s had moved into their respective positions within the ranks, and the different classes had taken on clear, fixed traits of personality. Some details were now commonly agreed upon. People acknowledged that those competing for the medal were effectively reduced to three—Hugh Carrow, Nell Harcourt, and Penrose Wilson; the recipient of the Avery scholarship remained less certain, as any member of a particular group of six might win it. A chubby, amusing, small boy from the up-country, who possessed a bumpy forehead and a mended coat, was viewed as virtually certain to capture the bronze medal for mathematics.
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0005 }

At the Academy that year, Opal Pettigrew was the most beautiful girl; among the Second Year classes, the beauty prize was won by Mabel Colby, though a minor yet discerning group preferred Nell Harcourt. Everyone qualified to judge agreed that Ethel Marr possessed the most fashionable hairstyles, while Odette Pullen—unassuming, hardworking, dutiful Odette—won top marks in domestic science. Flossie Tulk even achieved her own distinction for being the most caustic-tongued young woman attending Regent’s. Thus, one could justly claim that the former students of Miss Thorne maintained their prominence within the larger sphere of the academical curriculum.
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0006 }

Nell applied herself diligently and without pause. The competition between her and Hugh remained just as fierce as it was during their time at Brierley school, even if the rest of the class remained unaware of it, yet the resentment behind it had inexplicably vanished. Winning merely to triumph over Hugh was no longer Nell's goal; instead, she sought the honorable satisfaction of a hard-earned triumph against a respectable opponent. Succeeding would certainly be gratifying, but failing to do so no longer felt to her like an endurable existence was impossible.
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0007 }

Even with their studies, the pupils discovered chances to enjoy themselves. Nell passed a large portion of her free time at Beechwood, where she usually had her Sunday meals and accompanied Miss Pembroke to services. The old lady confessed that she was getting on in years, yet her dark eyes remained sharp, and her speech lost none of its original force. However, she refrained from directing her harsh words at Nell, who remained a special favorite of the discerning elder.
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0008 }

“That Nell-girl gets better continually,” she remarked. “Other girls weary me—they possess a sameness so annoying and endless. Nell possesses a rainbow’s many hues, with each hue being the most beautiful while present. I am uncertain if her ability to amuse matches her childhood days, yet she compels my affection, and my preference goes to those who compel my affection. Doing so spares me immense effort in forcing myself to feel affection for them.”
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0009 }

Then, nearly prior to anyone recognizing it, the arrival of spring occurred; over in Brierley, the Mayflowers were showing pink hues on the withered barrens where remnants of snow remained; and the woods and valleys bore the “mist of green.” However, inside Port Marlow, anxious Regent’s students concentrated their thoughts and conversations solely on examinations.
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0010 }

“It hardly seems believable that the term is almost at an end,” Nell said. “Why, during last fall it felt like such a long time ahead—an entire winter filled with studies and classes. And now here we stand, with the exams drawing near next week. Girls, at times I get the feeling that those exams are the only thing that matters, yet whenever I observe the large buds expanding on those chestnut trees and the hazy blue atmosphere at the street ends, they lose half of their significance.”
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0011 }

Odette, along with Opal and Flossie, who had paid a visit, held a different opinion on the matter. In their eyes, the approaching tests were perpetually of immense significance—much more critical than Maytime hazes or chestnut buds. While it was fine for Nell, who was certain to pass at minimum, to occasionally minimize their importance, one could not look at them dispassionately when one’s entire destiny hinged upon them, which the girls genuinely believed theirs did.
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0012 }

“In the past fortnight, I have dropped seven pounds,” Odette sighed. “Telling me not to fret is pointiess. I am going to fret. Fretting gives a little relief—as though you are taking action while you fret. Failing to obtain my certificate would be terrible, having attended Regent’s the whole winter and spent such a large sum of money.”
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0013 }

“It makes no difference to me,” Flossie Tulk declared. “Should I fail to pass during this year, I shall return for the following one. Paying for me to attend is well within my father's means. Nell, according to Frank Stockley, Professor Tremaine mentioned that Hugh Carrow was certain to receive the medal, whereas Emily Clay would probably be awarded the Avery scholarship.”
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0014 }

“Tomorrow that might cause me to feel badly, Flossie,” Nell laughed, “yet right now I genuinely believe that provided I am aware that the violets are blooming all purple down in the hollow under Grey Shutters and that small ferns are pushing their heads up in Lovers’ Lane, it does not matter very much whether I win the Avery or fail to. I have given my best effort and I am starting to grasp the meaning of the ‘joy of the strife.’ Second only to trying and succeeding, the finest thing is trying and losing. Girls, stop speaking about exams! Observe that arch of light green sky above those houses and imagine for yourself how it has to look above the purply-dark beech-woods behind Brierley.”
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0015 }

“Odette, what will you be wearing for commencement?” Opal inquired sensibly.
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0016 }

Odette and Flossie both replied simultaneously, and the conversation strayed into a secondary current regarding fashions. But Nell, resting her elbows on the window sill, placing her soft cheek against her interlocked hands, and having her eyes brimming with visions, gazed out without paying attention past city roof and spire toward that magnificent dome of sunset sky and fashioned her dreams of a potential future out of the golden fabric of youth’s inherent optimism. Every bit of the Beyond belonged to her, its possibilities hiding rosily within the approaching years—with every year being a rose of promise meant to be crafted into an everlasting chaplet.
{: #nw-v01-c35-p0017 }
